newsitem.title: USA: US cattle report points to higher summer supplies.
newsitem.headline: US cattle report points to higher summer supplies.

text.p: Friday's U.S. Department of Agriculture Cattle-on-Feed report points to increased fed cattle supplies and lower prices this summer, but little price change is expected Monday in CME live cattle futures, according to livestock analysts and participants on a CME panel.
"We are going to be looking at bigger supplies of fed cattle and marketings into the summer months," said panelist David Holloway, market analyst for Koch Beef Company.
Active marketings will keep live and futures prices firm before the large fed supplies press summer prices, he said.
USDA reported March 1 on-feed cattle supplies at 108 percent of last year in the seven major feedlot states which compared with average analyst estimates of 106.6 percent.

Total on-feed supplies include an adjustment to February on-feed numbers. February placements were 106 percent compared to the average estimate of 104.3 percent, and marketings for Febraury were 99 percent versus a 97.9 average estimate.

April CME live cattle futures could trade steady to 0.250 cent higher and back months steady to 0.100 lower based on the report. However, current cash market trends will likely have more influence on futures next week, trades and analysts said.

"I do not think this report will have much influence on Monday's (futures) opening. It could help the spread a little bit in favor of the April to the detriment of the June and August," said panelist Bob Price, livestock marketing economist for Cargill Investor Services Inc.

Longer-term price projections call for strength in futures and live markets into the spring and early summer before the increased fed cattle supplies come to market. This is a more seasonal type of price trend than was seen in 1996 when very high feed costs kept placements down.

"This year, the placement pattern is stacking itself up for a much more of a seasonal downturn in fed cattle prices into the summer months," said panelist James Mintert, an agricultural economist at Kansas State University.
Panelists and other livestock analysts agreed that prices will be strong before turning down in the summer.

"I would expect the fed market to trade back up into the upper $60s (per cwt)," Holloway said. "At least the market should challenge contract highs in the April (futures) and as we move into the summer the market probably will trade in the low $60s."

Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp, said, "The supply of cattle available for the slaughter market for the next 30 to 45 days is going to remain the tightest that we will see for the next several months."
